title: Signal Mirror
summary: Aim reflected sunlight at aircraft, boats, or distant searchers with a purpose-built or improvised mirror. A glass signal mirror is one of the longest-range daytime signals a survivor can carry, and it needs no batteries or fuel.

steps.title: Know when a mirror is your best signal
steps.body: A mirror works whenever the sun is out and you can see the target, or the part of the sky or horizon where a target might appear. It needs no batteries, makes no noise, and weighs about an ounce (28 g). Colorado Parks and Wildlife calls a glass military-style mirror the best daytime ground-to-air signal and says it can be seen 20 to 25 miles (32 to 40 km) away in good conditions; plan on 10 miles (16 km) or more as a safer working number. Haze, low sun, and thin overcast cut the range. A mirror is useless at night and in heavy overcast, so pair it with a light, whistle, and ground signal. Keep it on a lanyard around your neck so you can use it the moment you hear an engine.

steps.title: Get to open, high ground with a clear view
steps.body: Move to the most open spot you can safely reach: a clearing, ridge, shoreline, gravel bar, or rooftop. Trees and terrain block both the sun and your line of sight. Before you need the mirror, face the direction aircraft are most likely to come from, such as along a valley, road, river, or the route you filed in your trip plan. Note where the sun is. The mirror works best when the sun is in front of you or off to one side. When the sun is behind you, the angle is steep and aiming is harder, but it can still work. Stay put once you pick a good site - searchers find people who stay in one visible place much faster than people who keep moving.

steps.title: Aim a mirror that has a sighting hole
steps.body: Most commercial and military signal mirrors have a small hole or mesh grid in the center. Hold the mirror close to one eye, with the shiny side toward the target, and look at the target through the hole. You will see a small bright spot of light (often called the fireball) floating in the sighting grid or on your hand or face. Slowly tilt the mirror until that bright spot sits right on the target. The flash is now hitting the target. Keep the spot on the target and rock the mirror very slightly so the flash sweeps a little on either side. Read the instructions printed on the back of your mirror, because designs differ a little. Practice in your yard so you can do this in seconds.

steps.title: Aim an improvised mirror with the finger-V method
steps.body: Any flat, shiny surface works: a phone screen, CD, compass mirror, polished metal lid, or foil stretched over cardboard. Glass mirrors reflect much better than metal. Stretch your free arm out and make a V with two fingers. Line up the target inside the V. Hold the mirror near your face and tilt it until the reflected sunlight lands on your fingers. Then raise the light spot so it just passes through the gap of the V toward the target. Flicking the spot on and off your fingers makes a flash the observer can see. Another method is to hold your other palm in front of the mirror, find the light spot on your palm, then slide your palm out of the way while holding the angle toward the target.

steps.title: Sweep the horizon even when you see nothing
steps.body: The Army and Air Force survival manual advises sweeping the horizon with a mirror in non-combat survival situations. Pilots and boat crews may notice a flash before you can see or hear them. Every few minutes, slowly sweep the flash along the horizon and across likely flight paths and roads. When you do see an aircraft, aim straight at it and give a series of flashes. Groups of three flashes, then a pause, is a common distress pattern, but steady, repeated flashing on the target matters more than a perfect count. Keep signaling until the aircraft clearly responds. A pilot may rock the wings, circle, or flash lights to show they have seen you.

steps.title: Back off once you are spotted
steps.body: Once an aircraft has clearly seen you, stop holding the flash on the cockpit. A strong flash can dazzle the pilot, especially during a low pass or landing. Instead, flash only now and then, or follow any directions given by the crew over a loudspeaker or radio. Switch to body signals or ground symbols to pass simple messages, such as whether you need medical help. If the aircraft leaves without acknowledging you, keep sweeping every few minutes - search patterns often bring aircraft back over the same area.

steps.title: Carry and care for the mirror
steps.body: Keep a glass signal mirror with a sighting hole in every kit: day pack, vehicle kit, and go-bag. Store it in a sleeve so the face does not scratch. A cracked or scratched mirror still works but at shorter range. Clean it with a soft cloth. Practice twice a year on a sunny day by flashing a friend's house, a sign, or a distant tree. If you are hiding from people who could hurt you, remember that a mirror flash gives away your location. Cover the mirror when you are not using it.

warnings: Never flash a mirror into the eyes of drivers, pilots on final approach, or people nearby. A strong reflection can cause temporary blindness and a crash.
A mirror flash reveals your position to everyone who can see it. Cover it when not in use if hostile people may be nearby.
Do not rely on a mirror alone. It does nothing at night, in heavy overcast, or when the target is out of sight. Carry a whistle and a light too.
proTips: Glass military-style mirrors with a sighting grid outperform plastic and polished metal. They are inexpensive and weigh about an ounce.
Use a lanyard so you cannot drop the mirror while scrambling to aim at a passing aircraft.
Practice the finger-V method with your phone screen - it is the mirror you will most likely have if your kit is not with you.
A pilot may rock the wings in daylight to show they have seen you. Watch for it before you stop signaling.
source: FM 21-76-1 Survival, Evasion and Recovery / Colorado Parks and Wildlife

sources.title: FM 21-76-1 / AFTTP(I) 3-2.26 Survival, Evasion, and Recovery (Multiservice)

whenNotTo: At night or under heavy overcast - use a light, fire, or whistle instead.
When hostile people could see the flash and you are trying to stay hidden.
Toward road traffic or aircraft that are landing near you.

quickGlance.situation: It is daytime, the sun is out, and you need aircraft, boats, or distant searchers to notice you.
immediate: Move to the most open, high spot you can safely reach
Sight the target through the mirror's hole (or between a finger-V) and put the bright spot on it
Flash repeatedly at any aircraft, and sweep the horizon every few minutes when you see nothing
then: Once spotted, stop holding the flash on the cockpit and switch to body or ground signals
Keep the mirror on a lanyard and practice twice a year

title: Emergency Radio - NOAA and HAM Basics
summary: An overview of the radios that keep working when phones fail: what to listen to, which two-way radio services need a license, and what the FCC rules really say about calling for help. Start here, then read the detailed guide for each radio type.

steps.title: Listen first: NOAA Weather Radio and broadcast stations
steps.body: Receiving is always legal and usually the most useful thing a radio does in a disaster. NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts warnings, watches, forecasts, and non-weather emergency messages 24 hours a day on seven VHF frequencies from 162.400 to 162.550 MHz. The network has more than 900 transmitters, and most listeners are within about 50 miles (80 km) of one. A receiver with the Public Alert logo, SAME county coding, and battery backup will wake you for warnings. Also keep an AM/FM radio, because local stations carry official instructions, shelter locations, and road closures. A hand-crank or solar radio with NOAA, AM, and FM covers all three. See comms-013 for alert setup.

steps.title: Pick the right two-way radio for the job
steps.body: Four common services cover most family needs. FRS (Family Radio Service) handhelds need no license and suit short range within a neighborhood or campsite. GMRS uses the same frequency area with more power and repeaters, and needs an FCC license that covers your family; it costs $35 for 10 years with no test. CB (Citizens Band) needs no license and is common with truckers and off-roaders; channel 9 is set aside for emergencies and traveler help. Amateur (ham) radio needs a license with a written exam, but it reaches across town, across the state, or around the world. Each has its own guide: comms-007 (FRS/GMRS), comms-008 (CB), and comms-009 (ham).

steps.title: Get FRS channel and power facts right
steps.body: FRS has 22 channels, all shared with GMRS. Channels 1-7 and 15-22 allow up to 2 watts. Channels 8-14 are limited to 0.5 watt, and the FCC says their usual range is under half a mile. No FRS channel is reserved for emergencies or for any one user - the FCC page says users must share and listen before talking. Older advice that one FRS channel is an official emergency channel is wrong. Your family or neighborhood should agree ahead of time on which channel to use, and many groups pick channel 1 or 3 simply by habit. Write your chosen channel and privacy code (if any) in your family plan.

steps.title: Know the ham calling frequency and local repeaters
steps.body: Ham operators use calling frequencies where people listen for contacts. On the 2-meter band, 146.520 MHz FM is the widely used national simplex calling frequency (radio to radio, no repeater). Repeaters on hilltops or towers relay handheld signals across a county or more, and in disasters local groups such as ARES (Amateur Radio Emergency Service) often run organized nets on them. Look up your local repeaters and nets before an emergency, write them down, and program them into your radio. Anyone may listen to ham frequencies with a scanner or receiver; transmitting needs a license. See the repeater list in the app's reference section.

steps.title: Understand what the emergency rule really allows
steps.body: FCC rule 47 CFR 97.403 says nothing in the amateur rules stops an amateur station from using any means of radio communication at its disposal to send essential messages when life or property is under immediate threat and normal systems are not available. That rule is written for amateur stations. It is not a general permission for anyone to transmit on any frequency at any time. In a real life-or-death emergency with no other way to call for help, call for help on whatever radio you have, keep it short, and stop once help is on the way. Better yet, get licensed now so you can practice legally and know what you are doing when it counts.

steps.title: Use a simple distress call format
steps.body: On any radio: listen first so you do not talk over someone. Press and hold the talk button, wait one second, then speak slowly. Say 'Mayday, Mayday, Mayday' only for immediate danger to life; use 'Pan-pan' (three times) for urgent problems that are not yet life-threatening. Give who you are, where you are (address, landmarks, or GPS coordinates), what is wrong, how many people, and what help you need. Release the button and listen for at least 10 seconds. Repeat every few minutes. Marine VHF channel 16 is the distress channel for boats and is watched by the Coast Guard on coastal and many inland waters. comms-016 covers radio procedure in detail.

steps.title: Manage batteries and test monthly
steps.body: Radios draw far more current when transmitting than when listening, so listen most of the time and transmit briefly. Carry spare batteries of the right type, or a USB power bank and cable if your radio charges that way. Set a listening schedule with your group, for example the top of every hour for 10 minutes, so everyone can turn radios off in between. Test every radio once a month: check the battery, do a short radio check with a family member, and confirm NOAA reception. Keep a printed card in each radio bag with channels, frequencies, call signs, and your schedule.

warnings: No FRS channel is an official emergency channel. Do not count on strangers monitoring any particular channel.
Do not modify FRS radios or add power amplifiers to CB radios - both are illegal and can cause interference.
The FCC emergency rule in Part 97 applies to amateur stations. It does not give unlicensed people blanket permission to transmit anywhere.
Low-cost multi-band handhelds can transmit on frequencies you are not licensed for. Know what your radio is set to before pressing the button.
proTips: A weather radio with SAME coding lets you program only your county so it does not sound alarms for distant storms.
Agree on a family channel and a check-in schedule now - radios are useless if everyone is listening on different channels at different times.
Search for your county ARES or RACES group; they often welcome new licensees and can tell you which repeaters are used in disasters.
Keep a printed frequency card in each radio pouch. Phones and apps may be dead when you need it.
source: FCC Part 95 and Part 97 / NOAA NWS / ARRL

sources.title: 47 CFR 97.403 Safety of life and protection of property

whenNotTo: If 911 calls or texts still go through, use them first - radio is the backup, not the first choice.
Do not transmit on frequencies you are not licensed for just to chat or test during a disaster; it can block real emergency traffic.

quickGlance.situation: Phones are down or overloaded and you need official information or a way to reach family or help by radio.
immediate: Turn on NOAA Weather Radio (162.400-162.550 MHz) and a local AM/FM station for official instructions
Switch family radios to your pre-agreed channel and check in at the agreed time
For life-threatening emergencies with no phone, call 'Mayday' three times with who, where, what, and how many
then: Listen more than you transmit to save batteries
Get a GMRS license ($35, no test) or a ham license so you can practice legally before the next emergency

title: Signal Fire Construction
summary: Build and safely run signal fires that aircraft can see: flame at night and thick smoke by day. Three fires in a triangle is a recognized distress signal, but one well-placed, well-tended fire is far better than three that start a wildfire.

steps.title: Decide whether a signal fire is safe and needed
steps.body: A signal fire is for real emergencies when you need searchers or aircraft to find you. Before building one, look at the conditions. In dry grass, brush, or forest during high wind or drought, a signal fire can turn into a wildfire that kills you and the people coming to help. If the ground is very dry, keep the fire small, build it on rock, sand, gravel, or bare soil, and keep water or dirt ready to smother it. If you cannot control it, use a mirror, bright panels, ground symbols, a whistle, and a light instead. Respect fire bans except in a true life-or-death emergency.

steps.title: Pick an open, visible site
steps.body: Smoke and flame under thick trees are hard to see from the air. Move to the largest clearing you can safely reach: a meadow, ridge top, lakeshore, gravel bar, or open snowfield. Colorado Parks and Wildlife advises moving to a clearing where signals are easy to see, then staying there until searchers arrive. Clear a circle of bare ground about 10 feet (3 m) across around each fire pit, scraping away leaves, needles, and dry grass. Keep the fire well away from overhanging branches, tents, and your shelter. Stack your fuel upwind and at least several feet away from the pit so sparks do not light it early.

steps.title: Lay out three fire bases in a triangle
steps.body: Three fires in a triangle is a widely recognized call for help. Colorado Parks and Wildlife suggests building three fire bases about 30 to 50 feet (9 to 15 m) apart. Older manuals give larger spacing, but the key is that each fire is separate and the triangle shape is clear from the air. Keep one fire, at the top of the triangle, as your working camp fire that stays lit. Build the other two ready to light: dry tinder on the bottom, then dry kindling, then larger dry sticks. If you only have the fuel or energy for one fire, build one big, smoky fire in the most open spot - a single fire is still a strong signal.

steps.title: Stage smoke material and light on demand
steps.body: A fire burning for hours with no aircraft in sight wastes fuel and your energy. Keep the main fire going, and place a large pile of green leaves, fresh grass, green conifer boughs, or damp moss next to each base. When you hear or see an aircraft, light the two other bases from your main fire and pile green material on all three. Green material on a hot bed of coals makes thick white or gray smoke. Do not dump green material on a new, weak fire - it will smother it. Let each fire burn hot for several minutes before adding green fuel.

steps.title: Match the signal to the time and background
steps.body: At night, flame is the signal. Keep it bright and high with dry fuel, and skip the green material. During the day, smoke is the signal. White or gray smoke from green plants shows best against dark forest or rock. On snow, sand, or a bright, hazy sky, white smoke is harder to see; build bigger, use more fuel, and rely on movement and height of the column. The multiservice survival manual notes that dark smoke comes from tires and petroleum products. Burning rubber, oil, or plastic gives off toxic smoke and is hard to control, so treat it as a last resort only, downwind of people, on bare ground, and never in dry vegetation.

steps.title: Tend the fire and keep a lookout
steps.body: An unattended fire either dies or spreads. If you are in a group, assign one person at a time to watch the fire and listen for engines, and rotate every hour or two. Keep enough dry fuel stacked to keep the main fire going through the night. In mountain terrain, search flights often stop at dark, so daytime smoke and morning readiness matter most. In deserts and plains, searches may run around the clock, so keep flame ready at night. Use the fire alongside other signals - mirror, whistle, panels, and ground symbols - because no single signal is seen every time.

steps.title: Put it out completely when rescued or leaving
steps.body: When rescuers arrive or you move on, drown each fire with water, stir the ashes, and drown again until everything is cool to the touch. If you have no water, smother with dirt or sand and stir until no heat remains. Check for smoldering roots and embers outside the ring. Tell rescuers about any fire that is still burning so it can be dealt with. A signal fire that escapes later can still cause a wildfire after you are safe.

warnings: A signal fire that spreads can become a wildfire that blocks rescue and kills. Keep fires small enough to control, on bare ground, with water or dirt ready.
Burning tires, oil, or plastic releases toxic smoke and can flare out of control. Treat it as a true last resort, stand upwind, and never do it in dry vegetation.
Lighting a signal fire when you are not in trouble can trigger a costly search and may be illegal. Use it only in real emergencies.
Do not build fires inside or right next to your shelter. Smoke and carbon monoxide in an enclosed space can kill.
proTips: Keep your tinder for the two standby fires in a dry bag or under bark so it lights on the first try when you hear an engine.
Pre-cut and stack green boughs next to each base before you need them. You may have less than a minute of warning.
Practice making smoke on a legal campfire: add green material only after you have a hot coal bed.
Combine fire with a mirror and a bright panel. A pilot who sees smoke will look for something that confirms a person is there.
source: FM 21-76-1 Survival, Evasion and Recovery / Colorado Parks and Wildlife / USCG Navigation Rules Annex IV

sources.title: FM 21-76-1 / AFTTP(I) 3-2.26 Survival, Evasion, and Recovery (Multiservice)
Distress Signals (Rule 37 / Annex IV) study guide

whenNotTo: In very dry, windy conditions where you cannot control the fire - use a mirror, panels, and ground symbols instead.
When you are not actually in distress; a signal fire can launch a search.
Inside or right beside a shelter, vehicle, or building.

quickGlance.situation: You are lost or stranded and need aircraft or distant searchers to see you.
immediate: Move to a large clearing and scrape a 10-foot (3 m) bare circle for each fire
Keep one fire lit and build two more bases 30-50 ft (9-15 m) away to form a triangle
Stage green leaves or boughs next to each fire to make smoke when you hear an aircraft
then: Use bright flame at night and thick smoke by day
Tend the fire in shifts and drown it completely when you leave

title: Whistle Codes and Ground-to-Air Signals
summary: Use a whistle and simple sound codes to be found by nearby searchers, and lay out the core ground-to-air symbols that aircraft crews recognize. For panels, body signals, and full layout details, see comms-015.

steps.title: Carry the right whistle
steps.body: A loud whistle carries much farther than a shout and takes far less effort, which matters when you are cold, hurt, or out of breath. Choose a pealess whistle made of plastic: there is no ball inside to freeze, jam, or stick when wet. Test it in cold and wet conditions before you trust it. Clip one to every jacket, pack strap, life jacket, and child's backpack. Teach kids that the whistle is for emergencies only, and that blowing it when lost is the right thing to do. Boats under 12 meters (39 feet) are required by Coast Guard rules to carry a whistle or horn, so your boat kit should already have one.

steps.title: Use three blasts for help
steps.body: On land, three blasts of anything is the widely used call for help: three whistle blasts, three flashes, or three fires. Blow three strong blasts of about one to two seconds each, then stop and listen for a full minute. Repeat. If you are waiting a long time, blow a set every few minutes to save energy. Searchers often answer with two blasts, meaning 'I hear you, coming.' When you hear an answer, keep signaling at intervals so they can follow the sound to you. Many groups also use one blast to mean 'Where are you?' or 'Attention.' Agree on these meanings with your family and hiking partners ahead of time.

steps.title: Know the boating sound signals so you do not confuse them
steps.body: On the water, short and long blasts have set meanings under the Navigation Rules. One prolonged blast of four to six seconds means a vessel is leaving a dock or nearing a blind bend. Five or more short, rapid blasts is the danger signal: 'I do not understand your intentions' or 'danger.' A recognized distress signal for vessels is continuous sounding of any fog signal device, such as a horn held down without stopping. If you are on a boat in trouble, use continuous sounding, Mayday on VHF channel 16, and visual signals. If you are on shore near water, three blasts repeated still tells people you need help.

steps.title: Signal from inside buildings and rubble
steps.body: If you are trapped after a collapse, do not shout constantly - you will lose your voice and breathe in dust. Blow a whistle in sets of three, or tap three times on a pipe, beam, or wall with a hard object, then pause and listen. Rescue teams often call for quiet periods to listen for survivors, so signal when it goes quiet. Cover your mouth and nose with cloth to filter dust. Keep a whistle on your keychain or in your bedside kit for this reason.

steps.title: Lay out the core ground-to-air symbols
steps.body: Aircraft crews look for straight lines and sharp corners that do not occur in nature. These symbols are widely recognized: V means 'I need help' or 'require assistance.' X means 'I need medical help' or 'unable to proceed.' An arrow means 'I am going this way.' Y means 'yes,' and N means 'no,' for answering a pilot who asks a question over a loudspeaker. Colorado Parks and Wildlife suggests making symbols to attract attention about 30 to 50 feet (9 to 15 m) long and 3 to 4 feet (1 m) wide. Other symbol sets exist, but stick to these few; a crew may not recognize a rare symbol.

steps.title: Build symbols with strong contrast
steps.body: Use whatever contrasts with the ground: rocks on grass, dark branches on sand or snow, bright tarps, clothing, or a space blanket. In snow, stamp the lines deep or drag a log so shadows form, and line the trench with dark boughs. In grass, pull or flatten vegetation down to dark soil. Keep lines straight and corners sharp. Place symbols in the most open spot, away from tree shadows. Weigh down tarps and light items with rocks so a helicopter's rotor wash cannot throw them into people or the aircraft. When you leave a site, add an arrow pointing the way you went, and change or remove symbols once you are rescued so they do not start a new search.

steps.title: Combine signals and watch for a reply
steps.body: No one signal is seen or heard every time. When you hear an aircraft or searchers, use everything at once: whistle, mirror, waving bright clothing, and your ground symbol. A pilot who has seen you may rock the wings in daylight, or flash lights at night. Searchers on foot may answer your whistle with two blasts or shout back. Once contact is made, stay where you are unless told to move. Moving makes you harder to find.

warnings: Do not use gunfire as a signal unless it is your only option and you are certain of a safe backstop. Shots can be mistaken for hunters and can injure searchers.
Pea whistles can freeze or jam when wet. Test any whistle you plan to rely on in cold and wet conditions.
Weigh down tarps and light materials. Helicopter rotor wash can throw them into people or the aircraft.
Remove or change ground symbols once you are rescued so they do not trigger a second search.
proTips: Put a whistle on every child's jacket and teach them: stay put, blow three times, listen.
A whistle needs far less effort than shouting and works when your voice is gone - save your voice for talking to rescuers once they are close.
Stamp out a big V or X early, then use the rest of your energy on fire, shelter, and water.
Agree on simple whistle meanings with your group before every trip: one blast 'where are you,' two blasts 'coming,' three blasts 'help.'
source: Colorado Parks and Wildlife / USCG Navigation Rules / FM 21-76-1

sources.title: Lights, Sound and Distress Signals (training slides)
Distress Signals (Rule 37 / Annex IV) study guide

whenNotTo: When you are hiding from people who could hurt you - sound and ground symbols reveal your location.
Do not use boat danger signals (five short blasts) to mean 'help' - on the water they mean danger or confusion about another boat's intent.

quickGlance.situation: Searchers may be within earshot, or aircraft may fly over, and you need them to find you.
immediate: Blow three strong whistle blasts, then listen for a full minute; repeat every few minutes
Stamp or build a large V (need help) or X (need medical help) in the most open spot
When you hear an aircraft, use every signal at once: whistle, mirror, waving bright cloth
then: If someone answers with two blasts, keep signaling at intervals so they can home in
Stay put once contact is made unless rescuers tell you to move

title: Family Communication Plan and Out-of-Area Contact
summary: Build a simple, written family plan so everyone knows how to reach each other and where to meet when phones are jammed or the family is split up. Based on the FEMA Family Emergency Communication Plan.

steps.title: Collect the numbers on paper
steps.body: Phones die, get lost, or lock you out, and most people no longer remember phone numbers. Write down, on paper, the cell, work, and home numbers for every household member. Add the important people and places: schools and daycare, workplaces, doctors and pharmacy, a neighbor with a key, the vet, and utility and insurance companies. Note each child's school pickup and release rules, since many schools only release children to listed adults. Write any medical needs, allergies, and medications for each person. FEMA's family plan form is designed for exactly this list. Keep it to one or two pages so people will actually carry it.

steps.title: Choose an out-of-area contact
steps.body: Pick one person who lives outside your area, ideally in another state, to act as the family's message hub. During a local disaster, local lines are jammed, but a call or text to a distant number may still get through. Everyone in the family checks in with that person, who then passes messages along: who is safe, where they are, and where they are headed. Choose someone reliable who usually answers their phone, and pick a backup in case they cannot be reached. Ask both people first and give them a copy of your plan.

steps.title: Make texting the default
steps.body: FEMA's guidance is blunt: text is best. A text message needs much less network capacity than a voice call, and it often goes through when calls fail. Many phones will keep trying to send a text in the background until there is a gap in traffic. Agree on short, standard messages, for example: 'SAFE. At school gym. Staying until 6.' Make sure every family member knows how to send a text and a group text, including older relatives. Set up a group thread now with the whole household and the out-of-area contact. Keep voice calls for true emergencies and for times when texting will not work.

steps.title: Set meeting places at four distances
steps.body: Decide on places everyone knows: an indoor safe room at home for storms (an interior, windowless room on the lowest floor or a storm shelter); a neighborhood spot just outside the house for fires, such as a specific mailbox or a neighbor's porch; a place outside the neighborhood, like a library, community center, or house of worship, for when you cannot get home; and a place outside your town, such as a relative's or friend's home, with the address written down and routes discussed. Check that each place is accessible to everyone in your family and allows pets or service animals if needed.

steps.title: Save ICE contacts and set up phones
steps.body: In every phone, save at least one emergency contact labeled 'ICE' (In Case of Emergency), and tell that person about any medical issues. Set up the phone's emergency medical ID so it can be read from the lock screen, and add emergency contacts in the phone's safety settings - on newer phones these contacts can also be notified if you use satellite SOS. Turn on emergency alerts in notification settings. Enter all household and plan contacts into every phone, and create a contact group for the people you would need to reach in a disaster.

steps.title: Share it, carry it, post it
steps.body: Give each person a printed copy to keep in a wallet, purse, or backpack. Print a wallet card for kids and tape one inside their school bag. Post a copy in a central spot at home, such as inside a kitchen cabinet door. Put a copy in your go-bag and car. Check now and then that everyone still has their copy. Add your radio plan if your family uses radios: which channel, what time you check in, and call signs. A plan that only lives in one person's phone or head is not a plan.

steps.title: Practice and update every year
steps.body: Hold a short family meeting to walk through the plan. Have each person practice texting the out-of-area contact and sending a group text. Walk to the neighborhood meeting spot and talk through how each person would get to the out-of-town location. Have kids say key phone numbers from memory, and teach them that 911 is for life-threatening emergencies. Review the plan at least once a year, and whenever someone changes jobs, schools, or phone numbers. After a drill or a real event, talk about what worked and fix what did not.

warnings: Do not depend on phone contacts alone. A dead or lost phone takes every number with it - keep paper copies.
Do not tie up voice networks with non-emergency calls during a disaster. Text instead and keep calls short.
Confirm school and daycare release rules ahead of time. Children may not be released to adults not listed on file.
proTips: Laminate wallet cards or put them in a small zip bag so they survive rain and washing machines.
Write a standard check-in text on the card so stressed family members can copy it word for word.
Add a radio channel and a check-in time to the plan. It becomes your fallback when texting fails too (see comms-006).
Pick an out-of-area contact in a different time zone with care - choose someone who will answer at 3 a.m.
source: FEMA Family Emergency Communication Plan / Ready.gov

sources.title: Tips for Communicating in an Emergency (FCC/FEMA)

whenNotTo: Do not wait to check in with family before calling 911 for a life-threatening emergency - call 911 first.

quickGlance.situation: A disaster has hit, phones are jammed, and your family may be in different places.
immediate: Text your out-of-area contact and family group: SAFE, where you are, where you are going
Go to the agreed meeting place for the situation (home safe room, neighborhood spot, or out-of-town)
Keep any calls short; if a call fails, wait about 10 seconds before trying again
then: Check in at agreed times by text or radio until everyone is accounted for
Update the plan afterward with what worked and what did not

title: PACE Planning - Primary, Alternate, Contingency, Emergency Comms
summary: Use the PACE method from military and public-safety planning to give your family or group four independent ways to stay in touch, in a set order, with clear rules for when to switch. This keeps one failure from cutting everyone off.

steps.title: Understand the four layers
steps.body: PACE stands for Primary, Alternate, Contingency, and Emergency. The Primary is the best, normal method - usually the fastest and easiest. The Alternate is a common backup that is a little less convenient. The Contingency may be slower or less reliable, but it still gets the message through. The Emergency method is the last resort: often slow, inconvenient, or costly, but it works when everything else has failed. The U.S. Army popularized PACE, and CISA now promotes it for public-safety agencies. The same idea works for a household: you are deciding, before trouble, the order in which you will try each way of talking.

steps.title: Make each layer independent
steps.body: The goal is that one failure does not knock out more than one layer. Cell calls and cell texts both ride the same towers, so they are weak as Primary and Alternate together. A strong household plan mixes systems. Example: Primary - cell phone text. Alternate - internet messaging or Wi-Fi calling from a location that still has internet. Contingency - two-way radio (GMRS, FRS, or ham) on a set channel at set times. Emergency - satellite SOS or messaging, or a written note at a pre-agreed message spot plus going to a meeting place. Ask of each pair: if the power grid, cell towers, or internet fail, which of my layers still work?

steps.title: Plan for each pair of people and each situation
steps.body: A PACE plan is built for a specific task, not one plan for everything. Make one for the daily separation that worries you most - for example, parents at work and kids at school - and another for a long power outage at home, or a bug-out trip. For each, list who must talk to whom: parent to parent, parent to child, household to out-of-area contact. Some people may not have every tool. A young child may have no phone or radio, so their PACE may be: school staff, a teacher's phone, the school's reunification site, then the family meeting place.

steps.title: Set clear triggers to switch
steps.body: Everyone must know when to move to the next layer, or each person will sit on a different method waiting. Write simple triggers: 'If a text has not been answered in 30 minutes, switch to radio.' 'If the radio check-in at the top of the hour gets no answer twice, go to the meeting place.' 'If there is a city-wide outage, skip straight to the radio schedule.' Because the person receiving does not know which layer the sender is using, everyone should monitor more than one method when things go wrong - for example, keep the radio on while you wait for a text.

steps.title: Fill in the details each layer needs
steps.body: A layer is only real if the details are written down. For phones: numbers, the group text, and the out-of-area contact. For radio: radio type, channel or frequency, privacy code, call signs, and check-in times such as 10 minutes at the top of every hour. For satellite: which device or phone, who it sends to, and whether the service is active and paid. For the emergency layer: the address of each meeting place and a message spot, such as a note taped inside the back door or a marked rock at the end of the driveway. Put all of this on one printed card per person.

steps.title: Test every layer, not just the first
steps.body: A backup you have never used will fail when you need it. Once a month, run a quick drill: send the group text, do a radio check on your channel at the scheduled time, and confirm satellite devices are charged and subscriptions are active. Twice a year, run a full drill where you pretend the cell network is down, and work through Alternate, Contingency, and Emergency in order. Note what broke - a dead radio battery, a forgotten privacy code, an expired satellite plan - and fix it. CISA stresses that practicing PACE plans is what builds real resilience.

steps.title: Keep it simple and nest it in your bigger plan
steps.body: Four layers is the limit; more choices cause confusion under stress. Use the same channel numbers and check-in times across all your plans when you can. Tie your PACE plan into your family communication plan (comms-005), your rally points, and your evacuation plan so they agree with each other. Review it once a year or when people, phones, radios, or schools change. Share it with the out-of-area contact so they know how you may try to reach them.

warnings: Cell calls and cell texts share the same network. Do not count them as two independent layers.
Satellite services can lapse when a free period ends or a plan is suspended. Confirm status before relying on one as your emergency layer.
Do not build a plan around a radio you are not licensed to use or have never practiced with.
proTips: Write triggers as times, not feelings: '30 minutes with no reply' works better than 'if it seems bad.'
Use a single printed PACE card per person, with channels and times in large type.
Make the meeting place part of every plan's Emergency layer - walking there needs no electricity.
A note left at home with date, time, who, and where you went is a cheap, reliable last layer.
whenNotTo: In a life-threatening emergency, call or text 911 first - do not work through family PACE layers before getting help.

quickGlance.situation: Your normal way of reaching family has failed and you need to know what to try next and when.
immediate: Try your Primary (usually a text) and wait the agreed time
If no answer by the trigger time, switch to your Alternate, then Contingency (radio at check-in time)
Keep monitoring more than one method while you wait
then: If all else fails, use the Emergency layer: satellite device or go to the meeting place and leave a note
After the event, fix whatever layer failed

title: FRS and GMRS Radios - Rules, Licensing, and Real Range
summary: Choose and use family walkie-talkies legally. FRS needs no license; GMRS needs a $35, 10-year FCC license with no test that covers your family. Learn the channel and power limits, what range to really expect, and how repeaters help.

steps.title: Know the difference between FRS and GMRS
steps.body: FRS (Family Radio Service) and GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service) share the same UHF channels around 462 and 467 MHz, so FRS and GMRS radios can talk to each other on shared channels. FRS is licensed by rule: anyone of any age can use it with no paperwork, as long as the radio is FCC-certified and not modified. GMRS allows more power, detachable antennas, mobile and base radios, and repeaters, but the operator needs an individual FCC license. Most blister-pack walkie-talkies sold today are FRS. Radios labeled GMRS, or with removable antennas or more than 2 watts, generally need the license.

steps.title: Learn the FRS channel and power limits
steps.body: FRS has 22 channels. Channels 1-7 (462.5625-462.7125 MHz) and channels 15-22 (462.550-462.725 MHz) are limited to 2 watts. Channels 8-14 (467.5625-467.7125 MHz) are limited to 0.5 watt, and the FCC says their usual range is less than half a mile. All 22 channels are shared with licensed GMRS users. No channel is reserved for emergencies or for any one group, so listen before you talk and be ready to move. 'Privacy codes' (tones) only filter what your radio lets you hear - they do not stop anyone else from hearing you. FRS radios cannot be connected to the phone system.

steps.title: Get a GMRS license if you want more range
steps.body: A GMRS license costs $35 and lasts 10 years. There is no exam. You must be at least 18 and not a representative of a foreign government. One license covers your family members of any age, who can use radios in your licensed system. To apply, create an FCC Registration Number (FRN) in the FCC's CORES system, then apply for GMRS in the FCC's online License Manager and pay the fee. Your license gives you a call sign. You can renew during the 90 days before it expires; after it expires, you have to apply again. Identify with your call sign as the rules require - at the end of a series of transmissions and about every 15 minutes during long conversations.

steps.title: Use GMRS power and channels correctly
steps.body: GMRS main channels (462.550-462.725 MHz, the same frequencies as FRS 15-22) allow up to 50 watts for base and mobile radios and serve as repeater outputs. The 462 MHz interstitial channels (same as FRS 1-7) allow 5 watts. The 467 MHz interstitial channels (same as FRS 8-14) stay at 0.5 watt for handhelds with built-in antennas. The 467.550-467.725 MHz channels are repeater inputs only. A 5-watt GMRS handheld with a good antenna, or a 15-50 watt mobile radio in a vehicle, will clearly outperform a 2-watt FRS radio.

steps.title: Expect realistic range
steps.body: Ignore '35-mile' claims on the package; those assume mountaintop to mountaintop. UHF radio is mostly line of sight. Handheld to handheld in a neighborhood with houses and trees, expect roughly a half mile to two miles. Across open water or from a hilltop, expect more. Inside steel and concrete buildings, expect much less. The FCC says GMRS range is typically 1 to 25 miles depending on station type, terrain, and whether you use a repeater. To get more range: go higher, step outside or to a window, hold the radio upright, use a better antenna, and use a vehicle radio with a roof antenna.

steps.title: Use repeaters the right way
steps.body: A GMRS repeater on a tower or hill receives your signal on a 467 MHz input and re-sends it on a 462 MHz output, which can stretch handheld range to many miles. Many repeaters are run by clubs or individuals; ask the owner before using one and set the correct tone. The FCC prohibits linking GMRS repeaters through the internet or other networks to extend range. Repeaters often have backup power, but some go silent in long outages. Keep a simplex (radio-to-radio) channel in your plan as well.

steps.title: Set up a family radio plan
steps.body: Pick one main channel and one backup channel and write them, with any tone codes, on a card in each radio bag. Agree on check-in times, such as the top of every hour for 10 minutes, so radios can be off to save battery the rest of the time. Label every radio with its channel settings. Use rechargeable radios that can also take AA batteries, and keep spares. Test monthly by doing a radio check from the farthest place you are likely to be, such as a child's school or a neighbor's house.

warnings: Using a GMRS-only radio, more than 2 watts, or a detachable antenna without a GMRS license breaks FCC rules.
Privacy codes do not make conversations private. Assume anyone nearby can hear you.
Do not modify FRS radios. The FCC requires FRS radios to be certified and unmodified.
Package range claims are best-case. Test your real range before you rely on it.
proTips: One $35 GMRS license covers your whole family for 10 years - it is one of the cheapest upgrades in preparedness.
A mobile GMRS radio in the car with a roof antenna makes a strong base station during power outages.
Many families pick FRS/GMRS channel 1 or 3 as a habit, but write your own choice down - no channel is official.
Put the license call sign on a label on each radio so family members can identify correctly.

sources.title: FRS, GMRS and MURS frequencies and channel numbers
The FCC GMRS license fee has finally dropped

whenNotTo: When you need to reach people far beyond line of sight with no repeater - consider ham radio or satellite instead.
For private or sensitive information - FRS and GMRS are open channels.

quickGlance.situation: You need simple, short-range radio contact with family or neighbors when phones are down.
immediate: Turn radios to your pre-agreed channel and tone, and listen before talking
Get high or outside to improve range; hold the radio upright
Check in at your scheduled time and keep messages short
then: Get a GMRS license ($35, 10 years, no test) to use higher power and repeaters
Test real range from school, work, and neighbors' homes

title: CB Radio Basics and Emergency Channel 9
summary: Set up and use a Citizens Band (CB) radio, which needs no license, for road information and emergency help. Channel 9 is set aside by the FCC for emergencies and traveler assistance; channel 19 is where highway drivers talk.

steps.title: Know what CB is good for
steps.body: CB radio uses 40 channels between 26.965 and 27.405 MHz. The FCC requires no license, and anyone of any age may operate except a few groups such as foreign government representatives. CB is common with truck drivers, off-roaders, and rural neighbors, so it is a good way to ask for road conditions, report a crash on a highway, or reach nearby vehicles when cell service is out. CB is meant for short-distance talk. It is not private, and no channel belongs to any one person. Range is limited, so treat CB as a local tool, not a long-distance link.

steps.title: Learn the key channels
steps.body: Channel 9 is reserved by FCC rule for emergency communications and traveler assistance. Use it to report emergencies or ask for help, not for chat. Channel 19 is the traditional highway channel, where truckers share traffic, weather, and road hazard information; it is often the busiest channel and the most likely place to find someone listening on an interstate. By long habit, channels 16 and 36-40 are used for single sideband (SSB) on radios that support it. Emergency messages have priority on every channel - if someone breaks in with an emergency, stop talking and let them through.

steps.title: Respect the power and equipment rules
steps.body: CB radios are low power: 4 watts on AM or FM and 12 watts peak on SSB. The FCC forbids raising a CB transmitter's power or attaching a linear amplifier or any other power amplifier. Buy an FCC-certified radio and do not modify it. For base antennas on a building or tree, the top of the antenna may be no more than 20 feet (6 m) above the structure and no more than 60 feet (18 m) above the ground, with lower limits near airports. Vehicle and handheld antennas have no height limit. A properly tuned antenna does more for range than anything else you can legally do.

steps.title: Install and tune a vehicle CB
steps.body: A mobile CB in a vehicle is far better than a handheld because the vehicle gives it power and a larger antenna. Mount the antenna as high and as central as you can, usually on the roof or a sturdy bracket, and keep it clear of the cab. Run the coax cable without crushing or kinking it. Tune the antenna with an SWR meter, following the antenna maker's instructions, so the radio is not wasting power or getting damaged. Wire the radio to a fused power source. Keep a handheld CB with an extra battery in your kit as a backup if you must leave the vehicle.

steps.title: Expect realistic range
steps.body: With a good mobile antenna on flat ground, a few miles to roughly 5-15 miles between vehicles is typical. Handhelds with short antennas may reach only a mile or two. Hills, buildings, and noise from engines and power lines cut range. Sometimes conditions in the upper atmosphere carry CB signals hundreds of miles ('skip'), which can fill channels with distant stations - useful to know, but not something you can count on. If you cannot raise anyone, move to higher ground, try channel 19 as well as 9, and keep listening.

steps.title: Make an emergency call on channel 9
steps.body: Listen first. If the channel is clear, press and hold the mic button, wait a second, and speak slowly: 'Break channel 9, emergency.' Then give your location using highway number, direction of travel, mile marker or exit, and nearby landmarks. Describe what happened, how many people are hurt, and what help is needed. Ask whoever answers to call 911 for you. Release the button and listen. Repeat every minute or two if no one answers, and also try channel 19. Keep each transmission short. FCC rules limit continuous conversations to 5 minutes, followed by at least a 1-minute break, except for emergencies.

steps.title: Use good CB manners every day
steps.body: Practice on ordinary days so you know your radio when it matters. Keep the squelch set just above background hiss so you hear weak signals without constant noise. Use plain language - you do not need trucker slang. Do not swear, play music, or talk over others. Keep channel 9 clear except for real emergencies or travelers needing help. Some volunteer groups such as REACT have historically monitored channel 9, but coverage varies; never assume someone is always listening.

warnings: Linear amplifiers and modified CB radios are illegal and can cause serious interference to other services.
No one is guaranteed to be monitoring channel 9. If you can reach 911 by phone, do that first.
Do not mount a base antenna near power lines. Contact with power lines can kill.
Do not handle the mic while driving in heavy traffic; pull over safely first.
proTips: On interstates, channel 19 often gets a faster answer than channel 9 because more drivers are listening.
An SWR meter is cheap and saves your radio. Tune the antenna once and recheck after moving it.
Write your vehicle's normal routes and mile markers on your comms card so you can give a location quickly.
A CB with built-in NOAA weather channels gives you alerts on the road too.
source: FCC Part 95 Subpart D (Citizens Band Radio Service)
whenNotTo: When you need guaranteed contact or long range - CB is short-range and nobody is required to listen.
For private information - anyone can listen to CB.

quickGlance.situation: You are on the road or in a rural area with no cell service and need help or road information.
immediate: Turn to channel 9 (emergency) and listen; if clear, say 'Break channel 9, emergency'
Give highway, direction, mile marker or exit, what happened, and how many are hurt
If no answer, try channel 19 where truckers listen, and ask someone to call 911
then: Repeat every minute or two and move to higher ground if possible
Keep channel 9 clear for emergencies once you have help

title: Getting a Ham Radio License and Building a Go-Kit
summary: Earn an FCC amateur (ham) radio license and build a portable radio kit that works when phones and internet fail. Costs in 2026: about $15 for the exam at most ARRL VEC sessions (some teams charge less or nothing) plus a $35 FCC application fee, good for 10 years.

steps.title: Pick your starting license
steps.body: There are three U.S. license classes: Technician, General, and Amateur Extra. Start with Technician. It gives you full use of the VHF and UHF bands that handhelds and local repeaters use, which covers most local emergency work, plus limited privileges on some long-distance HF bands. General opens much more HF for statewide and nationwide contacts. No Morse code test is required for any class. There is no minimum age. The Technician exam is 35 multiple-choice questions drawn from a public question pool, and you need 26 correct to pass.

steps.title: Study the current question pool
steps.body: A new Technician question pool took effect for all exams starting July 1, 2026, and runs through June 30, 2030. It has 409 questions; 27 were added, 30 removed, and about 155 changed compared with the old pool. Make sure your book, app, or course says it covers the 2026-2030 pool. Older study materials based on the 2022 pool are out of date. Free practice exams are widely available online. Most people pass after two to four weeks of short daily study. Focus on understanding safety, rules, and basic electronics, not just memorizing answers.

steps.title: Get an FRN and register for an exam
steps.body: Before the exam, register in the FCC's CORES system to get a free FCC Registration Number (FRN). Exams are given by Volunteer Examiner (VE) teams working under a Volunteer Examiner Coordinator (VEC) such as the ARRL VEC. You can test in person at a local club or online through remote video sessions. Look up sessions on the ARRL website or other VEC sites and register ahead of time. Check what to bring - usually your FRN, a photo ID, and the session fee. At ARRL VEC sessions the fee is about $15; candidates under 18 pay a reduced $5. Some other VEC teams charge less or nothing.

steps.title: Pay the FCC fee and get your call sign
steps.body: The VE team does not collect the FCC fee. After you pass, the FCC emails you a link to pay the $35 application fee through CORES. You must pay within 10 calendar days or the application is dismissed, and the fee is not refunded if the application is dismissed. Once paid, your license and call sign usually appear in the FCC database within a few days; ARRL says 24 to 48 hours in many cases. The license lasts 10 years. Renewals and upgrades are also $35 per application. For new applicants under 18, the ARRL reimburses the $35 FCC fee after the license is issued.

steps.title: Start with a dual-band handheld and better antenna
steps.body: A dual-band (2-meter and 70-centimeter) handheld is the usual first radio. Low-cost models work, but choose one legal for amateur use and never transmit outside ham bands. Replace the short factory antenna with a longer, better one; this is the cheapest big improvement. Program your local repeaters, the 2-meter national simplex calling frequency (146.520 MHz), NOAA weather channels for listening, and your group's simplex frequency. Use free programming software and a cable, or the radio's keypad. Save a printed list of every channel. Then add a 25-50 watt mobile radio in your vehicle; it reaches much farther than a handheld.

steps.title: Build a go-kit in one bag
steps.body: Pack: handheld radio with two charged batteries, an AA battery case, and charger; a roll-up or telescoping antenna and a short length of coax with adapters; a mobile radio if you have one, with power cable and fuses; a 12-volt battery (lithium iron phosphate is light and long-lasting) and a small solar panel or car charger; earbuds or headset; printed frequency and repeater list, local net schedule, and your license copy; notebook, pencils, and message forms; headlamp; and a multi-tool. Keep it ready to grab. Check batteries monthly and charge after every use.

steps.title: Practice in nets and join a local group
steps.body: A license and radio are only half the skill. Check in to your local weekly repeater net to practice giving clear, short messages. Join your county ARES (Amateur Radio Emergency Service) or RACES group, or a local club, to learn how they work with emergency managers during disasters. Take part in practice events such as Field Day, where operators set up on emergency power. Under FCC rule 97.403, a licensed amateur may use any means at hand to send essential messages when life or property is in immediate danger and normal systems are down - practice now so you can do that well.

warnings: Do not transmit until your call sign appears in the FCC database. Until then you are not licensed.
Many low-cost handhelds can transmit outside ham bands. Using them on public-safety, business, or GMRS frequencies under a ham license is illegal.
Never let an antenna touch or come near power lines. Raise and lower masts with a spotter.
Pay the FCC fee within 10 days of the email or your application is dismissed with no refund.
proTips: Get your FRN before exam day - it saves time and avoids mistakes on the paperwork.
Study materials must cover the 2026-2030 Technician pool for exams from July 1, 2026 on.
A better antenna on a $30 handheld often beats an expensive radio with a stock antenna.
Practice running your go-kit on battery power for an evening. You will learn what you forgot to pack.

whenNotTo: If you only need to talk to family within a mile or two, FRS or GMRS is simpler and cheaper.
For private or encrypted traffic - ham radio rules generally prohibit messages meant to hide their meaning.

quickGlance.situation: You want long-range, infrastructure-free radio contact and need to get licensed and equipped.
immediate: Get a free FRN from the FCC and study the 2026-2030 Technician pool
Register for an exam session (about $15 at ARRL VEC; some free)
Pay the $35 FCC fee within 10 days of the FCC email
then: Program local repeaters and 146.520 MHz into a dual-band handheld with a better antenna
Build a go-kit and check in to a weekly net to practice

title: Off-Grid Text Messaging With Meshtastic LoRa Mesh Radios
summary: Set up small, low-power LoRa radios running free Meshtastic firmware so your group can text and share locations with no cell service, internet, or license. Each radio relays messages for the others, so the network grows with every node.

steps.title: Understand what Meshtastic does and does not do
steps.body: Meshtastic is free, open-source firmware for small LoRa radio boards. Each board pairs with your phone by Bluetooth (or connects by Wi-Fi or USB) and sends short text messages and position reports over the air, with no cell tower or internet. Every node that hears a new message re-broadcasts it after a short delay, so messages can hop across several radios to reach people out of direct range. Messages are short: the app limits them to about 200 characters. It is text only - no voice calls, photos, or video. Speeds are slow, so think of it as a reliable text pager, not a phone.

steps.title: Get compatible hardware
steps.body: Buy at least two (ideally one per person, plus one for a high spot) of a supported board listed on the Meshtastic website, in the frequency version for your country. In the U.S., buy the 915 MHz version; Meshtastic's U.S. region uses 902-928 MHz, a band shared by license-free devices. Boards are inexpensive compared with satellite devices, and there is no monthly fee. Choose models with a battery, a case, and ideally built-in GPS if you want location sharing. Always connect the antenna before powering on, because transmitting without an antenna can damage the radio.

steps.title: Flash firmware and set your region first
steps.body: Install current firmware using the Meshtastic web flasher, following the official instructions for your board. Then install the Meshtastic app (Android or iOS) or use the web client, and pair with the radio over Bluetooth. The first required step is setting the LoRa region - the radio will not transmit until you do. In the U.S., choose 'US.' Do not pick the ITU amateur regions unless you hold a ham license; in licensed mode encryption is not allowed and you must send your call sign. Give each node a clear name, such as 'DAD' or 'BASE,' so family can tell who is who.

steps.title: Keep everyone on the same preset and create a private channel
steps.body: Nodes must share the same modem preset to hear each other. The default preset, LongFast, balances range and speed and is what most local meshes use; leave it unless your local group uses another. Every radio ships with a default public channel encrypted with a well-known key, so anyone nearby on Meshtastic can read it. For family traffic, create a new channel in Settings, name it to generate a fresh 256-bit key, save it, and send it to the radio. Then share the channel's QR code with family members so their radios join the same private channel. Direct messages to one person are encrypted to that person's own key.

steps.title: Place nodes high for real range
steps.body: LoRa is line of sight. The app's estimate for LongFast is about 6 miles (10 km) in flat terrain with modest antennas, but handhelds in pockets, houses, and woods often reach far less - a mile or two is common. Height is the biggest factor. Meshtastic's documentation notes that a well-placed node on a rooftop or hilltop can outperform ground-level nodes even on slower, longer-range settings. Put one node in a high window, attic, or mast with a battery and small solar panel to act as your relay. The default hop limit is 3, meaning a message is re-sent up to three times; leave it unless you have a reason to change it.

steps.title: Send, confirm, and share location
steps.body: Type short, clear messages: who, what, where, and what you need. Watch the delivery status. For a direct message, 'Delivered to recipient' means the other radio acknowledged it - the strongest confirmation. 'Delivered to mesh' on a channel broadcast means it went out, but there is no per-person receipt. If you see 'Relayed, not confirmed,' wait and try again or move higher. Turn on position sharing only with people you trust, and set a sensible broadcast interval so batteries last. If you do not want your location shown, turn it off or use a fixed position.

steps.title: Power, test, and fit it into your PACE plan
steps.body: Charge every node and test monthly: send a message from each person's usual locations, like work, school, and a neighbor's home, and note what reaches and what does not. Carry a USB power bank and cable for each node; turn on power-saving mode on nodes that do not need to stay awake. Write your channel name, preset, and region on your comms card in case a radio has to be reset. Meshtastic makes a strong Contingency layer in a PACE plan: it does not depend on towers or the grid, but it does depend on charged radios and on nodes being within reach of each other.

warnings: Never power on a LoRa radio without its antenna attached. It can damage the transmitter.
The default channel uses a widely known key - anyone nearby with Meshtastic can read it. Use a private channel for family traffic.
Do not use amateur (ITU) regions without a ham license. In licensed mode encryption is prohibited.
Do not count on reaching 911 through Meshtastic. It only reaches other Meshtastic users.
proTips: A solar-powered relay node in an attic or on a pole can tie a whole neighborhood together.
Print the channel QR code and keep it in your go-bag so a new or reset radio can join in seconds.
Ask local Meshtastic groups which preset and channels they use - joining an existing mesh can greatly extend your range.
Keep messages short and standard: 'SAFE at home. Power out. Check in 1800.'
whenNotTo: To call for emergency services - use 911, a satellite SOS, or a PLB instead.
When you need voice contact or long range without relay nodes - use GMRS or ham radio.

quickGlance.situation: Cell and internet are down and your group needs to text and share locations nearby.
immediate: Power on the node (antenna attached) and connect the app by Bluetooth
Make sure region is US and you are on your family's private channel
Send a short check-in and watch for 'Delivered to recipient'
then: Move higher or place a relay node in a high spot if messages do not get through
Charge nodes from a power bank and keep check-ins short to save battery

title: Satellite SOS and Messaging - Phones, PLBs, and Satellite Messengers
summary: Know which satellite emergency options you already have and which are worth buying: iPhone and Pixel satellite SOS, carrier satellite texting, 406 MHz personal locator beacons, and two-way satellite messengers. Includes what each costs as of October 2026 and the limits that trip people up.

steps.title: Check what your phone can already do
steps.body: Many phones made since 2022 can reach emergency services by satellite when there is no cell or Wi-Fi signal. iPhone 14 and later (all models) have Emergency SOS via satellite in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, much of Western Europe, Japan, Australia, New Zealand, and a few other countries. Google Pixel 9 and later (except the Pixel 9a) have Satellite SOS in the U.S., Canada, Puerto Rico, Australia, and much of Europe. Some carriers, such as T-Mobile, add satellite texting to many recent phones. Open your phone's settings, search 'satellite,' and confirm the feature is listed and active before you head out.

steps.title: Know the costs as of October 2026
steps.body: Apple says Emergency SOS via satellite and Messages via satellite are free for two years after you activate an iPhone 14 or later; Apple has extended free periods for older iPhones before, so check the status in Settings. SMS sent through Messages via satellite may carry carrier fees. Google's Satellite SOS help page does not list a price. T-Mobile's T-Satellite costs $10 a month as an add-on or comes included with its top plan; AT&T and Verizon customers can add it for $10 a month with an unlocked phone and a free eSIM slot, and text-to-911 by satellite is described as free. A 406 MHz PLB has no subscription. Two-way satellite messengers need a paid plan.

steps.title: Practice with the demo before you need it
steps.body: Satellite SOS is harder than a normal text. Both Apple and Google offer a demo that walks you through pointing the phone at a satellite without contacting anyone. On iPhone, find the Satellite Connection demo in the Emergency SOS settings. On Pixel, go to Settings, then Safety and emergency, then Satellite SOS. Run the demo outside once, so you know how long it takes and what the screen asks you to do. Set up emergency contacts and your medical ID now; the phone can notify those contacts and share your answers and location when you use satellite SOS.

steps.title: Use phone satellite SOS correctly
steps.body: First, try calling 911 - the call may still connect on another carrier's tower. If it fails, the phone will offer a satellite option: Emergency Text via Satellite on iPhone, or Satellite SOS on Pixel. Tap it, then answer the short emergency questions with taps; they tell responders what is wrong. Choose whether to notify your emergency contacts. Go outside with a clear view of the sky and horizon, and follow the arrows to point the phone at the satellite. Hold still. Apple says a message can take about 30 seconds in ideal conditions and over a minute under light foliage. Stay connected and answer follow-up questions from responders.

steps.title: Understand the limits
steps.body: Satellite features only work when you have no cell or Wi-Fi coverage at all, and only with a clear view of the sky. Thick trees, canyons, buildings, and being indoors can block the signal. Phone satellite SOS is text only - no voice call. It is country-dependent, and iPhones bought in some countries do not support it. A phone also needs battery: cold, heat, and constant searching for a signal drain it fast. Carrier satellite texting can be slower than normal texting and may not support every app. None of these replace a dedicated beacon for people who travel often in remote country, fly, or boat offshore.

steps.title: Consider a personal locator beacon (PLB)
steps.body: A PLB sends a 406 MHz distress signal through the international Cospas-Sarsat satellite system to rescue coordination centers, with your GPS position. It works almost anywhere on Earth, needs no subscription, and has a battery that lasts years in standby. It is one-way: you cannot send details or know who is coming. Federal rules require you to register a 406 MHz beacon with NOAA. Registration is free at beaconregistration.noaa.gov, and NOAA asks you to confirm your details every two years. Update the registration if you sell the beacon or your contact information changes. Use it only for grave and imminent danger.

steps.title: Consider a two-way satellite messenger
steps.body: Satellite messengers such as Garmin inReach let you send an SOS to a monitoring center and then text back and forth with responders, family, and friends. They also offer tracking and weather. They require a paid subscription; published monthly plan prices for inReach range from about $8 to $50 depending on the plan. In 2026 Garmin changed its policy so that some newer inReach models (Mini 2, Mini 3, and certain watches) keep SOS access for up to 12 months while a plan is suspended. Check the current terms on the maker's website before you buy, since plans and policies change. Keep the device charged and test it before each trip.

warnings: Do not use satellite SOS or a PLB for anything less than a real emergency. False alerts send rescuers out and can bring penalties.
An unregistered 406 MHz beacon is illegal and slows rescue. Register it free with NOAA.
Free satellite periods and subscriptions can lapse. Confirm your service is active before every trip.
Satellite features need a clear view of the sky. Go outside and away from trees and walls before trying.
proTips: Run the phone's satellite demo in your backyard once - it removes the guesswork when you are scared and hurt.
Keep a PLB on your body, not in your pack, so it stays with you if you are separated from your gear.
Set emergency contacts in your phone so they get your location and status when you send a satellite SOS.
Carry a small power bank. A dead phone has no satellite feature at all.
source: Apple / Google / T-Mobile / NOAA SARSAT / Garmin

title: Using Your Phone When Networks Are Overloaded or Down
summary: Get messages through when cell networks are jammed or partly down, and keep your phone alive for days. Text first, keep calls short, use Wi-Fi when cell fails, and manage battery like it is your last one.

steps.title: Call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies
steps.body: During a disaster, 911 lines get flooded. Call 911 when someone's life is in danger, a crime is in progress, or there is a fire. For everything else, use local non-emergency numbers, 211 for community services, or official websites and social media. A 911 call from a cell phone will try any available carrier's network, so try it even if your own carrier shows no bars. Many areas now accept texts to 911, but not all; if text to 911 is not available, you will usually get an automatic reply telling you to call instead. If you can call, calling is still best because dispatchers can ask questions quickly.

steps.title: Text instead of calling
steps.body: A text needs far less network capacity than a voice call, so it often gets through when calls fail. FEMA's family plan guidance puts it simply: text is best. Your phone may keep trying to send a text in the background and deliver it when there is a gap in traffic. Keep texts short and complete: who you are, that you are safe or what you need, where you are, and your plan. Example: 'Ana - SAFE. At Lincoln School gym. Phone 30%. Will text 6pm.' Send one message to a group rather than many separate messages. Avoid sending photos and videos until networks recover; they use much more capacity.

steps.title: Keep calls short and wait before redialing
steps.body: If you must call, keep it brief and pass only essential information. The FCC and FEMA advise waiting about 10 seconds before redialing a call that did not connect, which helps reduce network jams for everyone. Do not keep hammering redial. Call your out-of-area contact rather than local family, since long-distance calls sometimes go through when local lines are overloaded. Update your voicemail greeting with your status and plan so callers get information even when you cannot answer.

steps.title: Use Wi-Fi calling and internet apps
steps.body: If cell towers are down but you can reach working Wi-Fi - at a shelter, library, business with a generator, or a neighbor with satellite or fiber internet - turn on Wi-Fi calling in your phone settings. Your phone can then send normal calls and texts over the internet. Internet messaging and social apps also work over Wi-Fi. Turn Wi-Fi calling on now and add your street address as the emergency address so 911 calls over Wi-Fi go to the right place. Many cities and carriers open free Wi-Fi hotspots after disasters; check official announcements on the radio.

steps.title: Stretch your battery
steps.body: Assume you will not be able to charge for days. Turn down screen brightness, close apps you are not using, and turn off Bluetooth and location for apps that do not need them. Turn on low power or battery saver mode. In areas with no signal, a phone burns battery searching for towers, so switch to airplane mode and turn it off only to check messages at set times - for example, five minutes at the top of every second hour. Keep the phone warm in cold weather, inside a jacket, because cold drains batteries quickly. Carry a charged power bank and cable.

steps.title: Charge safely when the power is out
steps.body: Charge from a power bank, a solar charger, or a hand-crank radio with USB output. You can charge in a car, but only with the vehicle parked outside in open air, never in a garage, even with the door open, because exhaust can kill you with carbon monoxide. Do not run a car or generator indoors to charge anything. If a charging station is open at a shelter or library, use it, and bring your own cable and a wall plug. Keep a basic non-cordless landline phone if you still have copper phone service; it may work during a power outage. Phones over internet or fiber service need power to work.

steps.title: Get official information and use satellite as a backup
steps.body: Keep emergency alerts turned on so your phone receives Wireless Emergency Alerts, which are free and do not count against texting limits. Use a battery or crank radio for broadcast news so you save phone battery. If you have no cell or Wi-Fi at all and an iPhone 14 or later, Messages via satellite (in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, and Japan) can send short texts to family; for emergencies, use Emergency SOS via satellite instead. Pixel 9 and later phones offer Satellite SOS. Some carriers add satellite texting. See comms-011 for how these work.

warnings: Never charge a phone in a car running in a garage or run a generator indoors. Carbon monoxide kills.
Do not tie up 911 with non-emergency questions during disasters. Use 211, local non-emergency lines, or official websites.
Do not text or call while driving in disaster traffic. Pull over safely first.
proTips: Turn on Wi-Fi calling and set your emergency address now - it takes two minutes and can save hours later.
Write a standard check-in text on your family card so everyone sends the same clear information.
Airplane mode plus scheduled check-ins can make a phone battery last several days.
Download offline maps and save key documents to your phone before storm season.
