title: Emergency Alerts - WEA, EAS, NOAA Weather Radio and SAME Codes
summary: Make sure official warnings reach you through at least two paths: Wireless Emergency Alerts on your phone, the Emergency Alert System on radio and TV, and a NOAA Weather Radio programmed with SAME codes for your county. All are free once you own the device.

steps.title: Know the three main alert paths
steps.body: Officials send warnings through FEMA's Integrated Public Alert and Warning System (IPAWS). Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA) go to cell phones in the affected area. The Emergency Alert System (EAS) breaks into radio, TV, and cable programs. NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards broadcasts National Weather Service warnings and other civil emergency messages 24 hours a day, and its digital SAME codes are also used by broadcasters for EAS. Each path can fail - a phone can be off or out of range, TV needs power, and a weather radio can be out of range of its transmitter - so set up at least two, especially for nighttime warnings.

steps.title: Turn on Wireless Emergency Alerts
steps.body: WEA messages look like texts but use a special tone and vibration that repeats twice. They are free, need no sign-up, and do not count against texting limits. Officials do not need your phone number or personal information; alerts go to every compatible phone near the cell towers in the warning area. Types include National alerts, Imminent Threat alerts (extreme weather, active shooters, and other current dangers), AMBER alerts for child abductions, Public Safety alerts, and opt-in Test alerts. Newer phones show up to 360 characters. Spanish alerts are supported and display based on your phone's language setting. Check your phone's notification settings to confirm alerts are on.

steps.title: Use radio and TV for details
steps.body: WEA messages are short. They tell you what is happening and what to do right now, but often say to check local media. EAS alerts on radio and TV give more detail, and local stations usually stay on the air with updates during major events. Keep a battery or hand-crank AM/FM radio, since TV and internet may be out. In a car, the radio is often the fastest source. Note the call letters of your local emergency stations on your family plan.

steps.title: Buy the right weather radio
steps.body: Look for a receiver with the Public Alert logo. The National Weather Service recommends these features: a tone alarm that wakes you, SAME technology so you get only alerts for your area, selectable alert types so you can turn off messages you do not need, battery backup for power outages, and an external antenna jack for fringe areas. Prices run about $20 to $200. Place the radio where you will hear it at night, such as a bedroom or hallway. Hand-crank radios with a NOAA band are good backups but often lack SAME and alarm features.

steps.title: Program SAME codes for your county
steps.body: SAME (Specific Area Message Encoding) codes are six digits. The first digit is 0 for a whole county, or another number for part of a county. The next two digits are the state, and the last three are the county. Find your codes on the NWS SAME location codes page on weather.gov, or by calling 1-888-NWR-SAME (1-888-697-7263). Enter the code for your county, plus nearby counties where storms often come from or where family members live or work. Follow your radio's manual. Set the radio to the frequency for the transmitter that serves your county.

steps.title: Pick the right frequency and test it
steps.body: NOAA Weather Radio uses seven frequencies: 162.400, 162.425, 162.450, 162.475, 162.500, 162.525, and 162.550 MHz. There are more than 900 transmitters, and most listeners are within about 50 miles (80 km) of one, though terrain can change that. Use the frequency listed for your county's transmitter, even if another station sounds louder or clearer - the NWS warns not to program a station that is not assigned to your SAME area. Transmitters send routine tests on a set schedule that your local NWS office posts; check that your radio alarms during a test. Replace backup batteries once a year.

steps.title: Act on the alert
steps.body: When an alert sounds, read or listen to the whole message. Note the type (warning means act now; watch means be ready), the area, the expiration time, and the instructions. A long 1050 Hz tone on a weather radio comes before the message; a short burst of digital noise marks the end. Follow the instructions right away: shelter in place, move to your safe room, or evacuate as directed. Then use radio or local news for updates, and text your family a short status message. Do not wait to see the danger before acting - tornado and flash flood warnings may give only minutes.

warnings: Do not rely on a single alert path. Phones can be off, silenced, or out of range, especially at night.
Do not program your weather radio for a louder station that is not assigned to your county; you may miss local warnings.
Do not turn off Imminent Threat alerts to avoid noise. They carry the most urgent life-safety warnings.
proTips: Program SAME codes for counties upwind of you so you get a few extra minutes of warning on approaching storms.
Put a weather radio in each bedroom hallway in tornado country - it is the best wake-up warning at night.
Leave your phone's emergency alerts on and its ringer settings so alerts can sound even in Do Not Disturb mode, if your phone allows it.
Sign up for your county's local alert system too; it often sends warnings that do not go out over WEA.
source: FEMA IPAWS / NOAA National Weather Service
whenNotTo: Do not wait for an alert if you can already see or hear danger, such as rising water or a roaring wind. Act now.

quickGlance.situation: You want to be sure official warnings reach you, day or night, even if the power or phone network fails.
immediate: Confirm Wireless Emergency Alerts are on in your phone settings
Program a Public Alert weather radio with your county's 6-digit SAME code and assigned frequency
Keep a battery or crank AM/FM radio for details and updates
then: Check that the radio alarms during a scheduled test and replace backup batteries yearly
When an alert sounds, read the whole message and follow its instructions right away

title: Morse Code Basics for Emergencies
summary: Send and recognize SOS and a few key letters in Morse code with a flashlight, whistle, horn, or by tapping. SOS in Morse is a recognized international distress signal, and it works when voice and phones do not.

steps.title: Learn SOS first
steps.body: SOS is three short, three long, three short: dot-dot-dot, dash-dash-dash, dot-dot-dot. It is listed among the recognized distress signals in the international rules for vessels, and it is understood by aircrews and rescuers worldwide. Send it as one continuous group with no long pauses between the S, O, and S, then pause for a few seconds and repeat. Do not worry about perfect speed. A slow, clear, steady SOS is far better than a fast, sloppy one. Practice tapping it on a table until you can do it without thinking.

steps.title: Get the timing right
steps.body: Morse code is built on a simple rhythm. A dot is one unit long. A dash is three units. The gap between parts of the same letter is one unit. The gap between letters is three units. The gap between words is seven units. For a flashlight, a good beginner unit is about half a second, so a dot is a quick blink and a dash is a held beam of about one and a half seconds. The GridDown app's Morse player uses these same ratios at a faster practice speed, so you can watch and copy the pattern.

steps.title: Signal with a light
steps.body: At night, a flashlight, headlamp, phone light, or vehicle headlights can carry Morse code for miles. Point the light directly at the searcher, aircraft, or boat, and keep your hand steady. Use the switch or cover the lens with your hand to make clean on and off flashes - switch-blinking can be faster and sharper with a hand or hat over the light. Avoid shining bright light into anyone's eyes at close range, and never into a pilot's eyes during landing. In daylight, a signal mirror can send Morse by tilting the flash on and off the target.

steps.title: Signal with sound and tapping
steps.body: A whistle, car horn, or air horn can send Morse in the open. Short blasts are dots and longer blasts are dashes, with the same gaps as light. If you are trapped in rubble or a building, tap SOS on a pipe, beam, or wall with a hard object - rescuers listen for tapping during quiet periods. Tap three quick, three slow (spaced), three quick, then stop and listen for at least a minute. On land, plain groups of three blasts also mean help, and most people recognize that pattern even if they do not know Morse.

steps.title: Learn a few useful letters
steps.body: Beyond SOS, a few letters make simple messages possible. E is one dot. T is one dash. A is dot-dash. N is dash-dot. I is dot-dot. M is dash-dash. K is dash-dot-dash and means 'go ahead' or 'over' in radio Morse. R is dot-dash-dot and means 'received.' Numbers have five parts: 1 is dot followed by four dashes, and 5 is five dots. The full alphabet is in the GridDown Signaling screen. Spell out short words such as 'HURT,' 'WATER,' or a number of people, and send them slowly.

steps.title: Learn by sound, then practice weekly
steps.body: People who learn Morse by sound, not by looking at charts of dots and dashes, get faster and make fewer mistakes. Use a free practice app or website that plays letters at full speed with long gaps between them (the Farnsworth method), and add letters a few at a time. Ten minutes a day for a few weeks will get you sending and receiving simple words. Practice sending with a flashlight to a family member across a yard or field. Morse code is no longer required for any U.S. ham license, but many licensed hams still use it on the air because it gets through weak conditions where voice fails.

steps.title: Know when Morse is the right tool
steps.body: Use Morse when you can be seen or heard but cannot talk: at night across a valley, from a boat to shore, to an aircraft overhead, or trapped and tapping. Use plain voice, a phone, or a radio when they work, because they are faster and clearer. Remember that most people outside radio and rescue circles cannot read Morse beyond SOS, so keep messages to SOS or very short words. Combine Morse with other signals, such as a fire, a ground symbol, or a strobe, for the best chance of being noticed.

warnings: Do not flash bright lights into the eyes of drivers or pilots who are close or landing. You can blind them.
Use SOS only for real distress. A false SOS can launch a search and may be illegal on radio or at sea.
If you are trapped, do not shout constantly. Tap and whistle in sets, and save your energy and air.
proTips: Practice tapping SOS on a steering wheel or table until it is automatic.
A headlamp with a momentary button makes the cleanest light Morse.
Keep messages short. Most rescuers know SOS; few can read long Morse messages.
Use the GridDown Morse player to watch the rhythm, then copy it with your own light.
source: International distress signals (COLREGS Annex IV) / ARRL

title: Signal Panels, Body Signals, and Ground-to-Air Signals
summary: A complete visual signaling plan for being found from the air: bright panels like the VS-17, ground symbols, body signals, rooftop messages, lights, and smoke. It pulls together the methods on the GridDown Signaling screen and shows how to combine them.

steps.title: Think like the pilot
steps.body: From the air, people are tiny and nature is full of random shapes. Crews notice three things: contrast (bright color on dark ground, dark on light), straight lines and sharp corners that nature does not make, and movement or flashes. Your job is to give them all three in the most open spot you can find. Pick a clearing, ridge, beach, gravel bar, road, parking lot, or rooftop and stay there. The military survival manual stresses making pattern signals as large as possible, with straight lines, sharp corners, and strong color or shadow contrast. Prepare signals early, while you have daylight and energy, so they are ready the moment you hear an engine.

steps.title: Lay out a signal panel such as the VS-17
steps.body: The VS-17 is a military signal panel: lightweight nylon, fluorescent orange on one side and cerise (pink-red) on the other. Any large, bright tarp, emergency blanket, raincoat, or boat cover can work the same way. Spread the panel flat and tight in the open, fully unfolded, with rocks or stakes on the corners so wind and rotor wash cannot lift it. Use the side that contrasts most with the ground. If you have two panels or a long tarp, lay them as a large X or V. Movement catches the eye, so when you hear an aircraft, grab one corner and wave or flip the panel. For boats, an orange flag at least 3 by 3 feet with a black square and black ball is a recognized daytime distress signal.

steps.title: Build ground symbols that mean something
steps.body: Use the core symbols most crews recognize: V means 'I need help.' X means 'I need medical help' or 'unable to proceed.' An arrow means 'I went this way.' Y means 'yes' and N means 'no' when a crew asks you questions by loudspeaker. Colorado Parks and Wildlife suggests symbols 30 to 50 feet (9 to 15 m) long and 3 to 4 feet (1 m) wide to attract attention; the UK Scouts teach about 10 by 3 meters with 3 meters between symbols. Bigger is better. Build with rocks, logs, branches, clothing, or trenches dug or stamped into snow, sand, or grass. Avoid rare or made-up symbols; a crew may not know them.

steps.title: Use body signals
steps.body: When an aircraft is close enough to see you, your body becomes a signal. Stand in the open where your outline shows against the ground. Slowly and repeatedly raising and lowering your outstretched arms to your sides is a recognized distress signal under the international rules for vessels and is widely understood by aircrews. Wave bright clothing or a panel to add color and movement. Do not wave casually, which can look like a friendly hello. Watch for the reply: in daylight a pilot who has seen you may rock the wings side to side; in low light the aircraft may flash green lights or turn its landing lights on and off twice.

steps.title: Signal from a rooftop or city
steps.body: In floods, earthquakes, and hurricanes, many people are rescued from roofs and upper floors by helicopter. Paint, spray, tape, or lay out large letters on the roof or a flat surface: HELP or SOS, with letters at least 8 to 10 feet (2.5 to 3 m) tall in a color that contrasts with the roof. Add an arrow pointing to where you are if you are not on the roof. Hang bright sheets or towels from windows and balconies. In daylight, use a mirror or a phone screen to flash at helicopters. At night, flash a light toward the sound of engines. Tell rescuers about injured people by adding an X or writing a number, such as '3 HURT.'

steps.title: Use lights at night
steps.body: At night, a light is the best visual signal. A strobe flashing toward aircraft or boats stands out far better than a steady beam. Flash a flashlight or headlamp in groups of three, or send SOS in Morse code (three short, three long, three short). Aim at the aircraft, not at the clouds. For boats, an electric distress light that automatically flashes SOS is a Coast Guard-approved night distress signal. Turn lights on early and conserve batteries by signaling when you hear or see an aircraft. The military manual notes that some strobes give one extra flash when turned off, so expect that.

steps.title: Add smoke, fire, flares, and dye
steps.body: By day, smoke columns are visible for miles. Thick white smoke from green vegetation on a hot fire works against dark forest; see comms-003 for building signal fires safely. Orange smoke signals, sold for boats, are a recognized daytime distress signal and show well against water and snow. Use flares and smoke only when an aircraft or boat is in sight or close, because they burn out in seconds to minutes. Hold handheld flares downwind and away from your body and boat. At sea, sea dye marker colors the water around you, but it disperses quickly in rough water, so use it when rescuers are near.

steps.title: Combine signals and maintain them
steps.body: No single signal is seen every time, so layer them: a panel or ground symbol always laid out, a mirror or light ready in your hand, and a fire or smoke ready to light. Repair symbols after wind, rain, or snow. Remove or change your symbols once you are rescued or leave, and add an arrow if you move, so searchers are not misled. In a group, assign one person at a time as lookout and signaler. If you are worried about people who could harm you finding you, weigh the risk - visual signals reveal your position to everyone, not just rescuers.

warnings: Weigh down every panel, tarp, and symbol material. Helicopter rotor wash can throw loose items into people or the aircraft.
Flares and smoke signals are hot and can start fires or burn you. Hold them downwind and away from fuel, people, and dry grass.
Never shine bright lights or flash mirrors into the cockpit of an aircraft that is landing or hovering near you.
Remove or change ground signals after rescue so they do not start a new search.
proTips: Keep a fluorescent orange tarp or panel in every vehicle and go-bag - it doubles as shelter and a signal.
Lay out your V or X first thing in the morning; then work on water, shelter, and fire.
In snow, stamp symbols deep so shadows show, then line the trenches with dark branches.
Practice your rooftop plan: know where you would get paint or tape and how you would get onto the roof safely.

Do not light flares or smoke in dry vegetation or near fuel.
Do not use made-up symbols in place of the core V, X, arrow, Y, and N - crews may not recognize them.

immediate: Lay a bright panel or tarp flat in the open, weighted at the corners
Build a large V (need help) or X (need medical help) with strong contrast

title: Radio Procedure - Prowords, Phonetic Alphabet, and Clear Emergency Messages
summary: Talk on any radio so people understand you the first time: listen before you transmit, use standard prowords and the phonetic alphabet, and give emergency messages in a fixed order. Works on FRS, GMRS, CB, ham, and marine VHF.

steps.title: Think, listen, then talk
steps.body: Only one person can talk on a channel at a time, and anyone who presses the button blocks everyone else. Before you transmit, decide exactly what you will say - write it down if you can. Listen for a few seconds to make sure the channel is clear. Press and hold the talk button, wait about one second so the first word is not cut off, then speak slowly and clearly in a normal voice with the microphone a couple of inches from your mouth. Keep each transmission short, then release the button and listen. Never hold the button down while you think.

steps.title: Use the basic prowords
steps.body: Prowords are standard words that save time and prevent confusion. 'This is' comes before your own name or call sign. 'Over' means 'I am done talking and expect a reply.' 'Out' means 'I am done and expect no reply' - only the person who started the call should say it, and never say 'over and out.' 'Roger' means 'I received your message.' 'Wilco' means 'I will comply.' 'Say again' asks someone to repeat. 'Break' marks a pause between parts of a message or asks to interrupt. 'Affirmative' and 'negative' mean yes and no and are easier to hear than 'yeah' and 'nah.' 'Standby' means wait.

steps.title: Spell with the phonetic alphabet
steps.body: Letters like B, D, E, and P sound alike over a radio. Spell names, street names, and call signs using the international phonetic alphabet: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel, India, Juliett, Kilo, Lima, Mike, November, Oscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo, Sierra, Tango, Uniform, Victor, Whiskey, X-ray, Yankee, Zulu. Say numbers digit by digit: 'one two five,' not 'one twenty-five.' Many radio users say 'niner' for 9 so it is not confused with 'five.' Example: 'Elm Street, I spell: Echo Lima Mike.' Print the alphabet on your radio card and practice spelling your own name.

steps.title: Make a normal call
steps.body: Say the name or call sign of the station you want, then 'this is' and your own name or call sign, then 'over.' Example: 'Base, Base, this is Mom, over.' Wait for the answer. When they reply, give your message in short pieces. On busy channels, move to an agreed working channel once you have made contact so the calling channel stays clear. On marine VHF, for example, boaters call on channel 16 and then switch to a working channel such as 68, 69, 71, 72, or 78. Never request a radio check on marine channel 16. Use plain English rather than codes - '10-codes' mean different things to different groups.

steps.title: Use distress and urgency calls correctly
steps.body: There are three priority calls, used worldwide on marine radio and understood on most radios. 'Mayday' (said three times) means grave and immediate danger to life or a vessel. 'Pan-pan' (pronounced 'pahn-pahn,' said three times) means urgent but not immediately life-threatening, such as a disabled boat drifting or a broken leg with no immediate danger. 'Securite' (pronounced 'say-cure-ee-tay,' said three times) means a safety message such as a hazard to others. If a pan-pan situation gets worse, upgrade it to mayday. Any station that hears a mayday should stop transmitting except to help.

steps.title: Give an emergency message in a fixed order
steps.body: Use this order so the listener can write it down: 1) 'Mayday, Mayday, Mayday.' 2) 'This is' and your name, call sign, or vessel name, three times. 3) Your location: address, crossroads, mile marker, landmarks, or latitude and longitude. 4) What is wrong: fire, crash, flood, injury. 5) How many people, and how many are hurt. 6) What help you need. 7) A description that helps rescuers find you, such as vehicle color or 'orange tarp on roof.' 8) 'Over.' Then release the button and listen for 10 to 15 seconds. If no one answers, repeat. Location is the most important piece - say it twice.

steps.title: Confirm and pass messages for others
steps.body: When you receive important information, read back the key parts - especially numbers, names, and locations - so the sender can catch mistakes. Example: 'Roger, three people, one injured, at 125 Elm, Echo Lima Mike, over.' If you relay a message for someone, write it down first and pass it word for word, with who it is from and the time. Keep a simple log with time, who you talked to, and what was said; it helps rescuers and keeps your group from losing track.

steps.title: Practice until it is automatic
steps.body: Under stress, people forget words, talk too fast, and leave out their location. Practice with your family or group during monthly radio checks: each person makes a call, gives a pretend emergency message in the fixed order, and the other person reads it back. Tape a printed message card with the order and the phonetic alphabet inside each radio bag and near your base radio. Check in to a local ham or GMRS net if you are licensed - it is the best practice you can get.

warnings: Never send a false Mayday. It is a federal crime on marine radio and can divert rescuers from real emergencies.
Do not keep the talk button pressed while thinking or after speaking. You block everyone else, including people calling for help.
Do not give your location vaguely. 'By the lake' can mean miles; give crossroads, landmarks, or coordinates.
proTips: Write your location in the fixed message order before you press the button. Read it, do not improvise.
Say your location twice - it is the part most often missed.
Keep a laminated card with the message order and phonetic alphabet in every radio bag.
Count 'one-thousand-one' after pressing the button before speaking so your first word is not cut off.
